title: Jerusalem Falls
summary: After a siege of about eighteen months, Babylon breaks through Jerusalem's wall. Zedekiah flees by night, is captured near Jericho, sees his sons killed at Riblah, and is blinded and taken to Babylon in chains; the city is burned and its people deported, while the poorest are left with fields and vineyards. Jeremiah is released into the care of Gedaliah, and a word given earlier promises Ebed-melech his life because he trusted in God.
story: Everything Jeremiah has warned of for forty years happens in this chapter, and the narrator tells it with almost no comment. The prophet's hearers have heard the choice set before them again and again, most recently in 38:17-23, and now the consequences arrive exactly as he described them. The chapter is a hinge in the whole Old Testament story: the line of David loses its throne, the city God chose is burned, and the people are taken from the land promised to Abraham. Yet two small notes of mercy frame the end. Jeremiah, the man everyone tried to silence, is set free, and Ebed-melech, the foreigner who pulled him from the cistern, is promised he will live. The story continues in chapter 40 among the survivors left in the land.
historical:
The siege began in the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, about January 588 BC, and the wall was breached on the ninth day of the fourth month of his eleventh year, in July (verses 1 and 2). Scholars divide over whether that summer was 587 or 586 BC, because the ancient ways of counting regnal years can be reckoned more than one way. The same events are told in 2 Kings 25 and again in Jeremiah 52, both of which add that the temple and city were burned a month later. The Babylonian Chronicle, which records the earlier capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC, has a gap after 594 BC in its surviving tablets, so the Babylonian account of this siege has not been found. Excavations in Jerusalem have uncovered destruction layers from this period with ash, collapsed buildings, and arrowheads, consistent with a city taken and burned.

The Babylonian officers in verse 3 bear real Babylonian names and titles, though the Hebrew text is hard to divide and scholars read the list differently. Rabsaris is a title meaning chief official (often associated with eunuchs), and Rabmag is a high title of uncertain meaning. In 2007 the Assyriologist Michael Jursa identified a cuneiform tablet in the British Museum, dated to about 595 BC, that mentions a chief official named Nabu-sharrussu-ukin; many scholars take him to be the Nebo-sarsekim of verse 3, though some question the match. Nergal-sharezer may be the man who later became king of Babylon (Neriglissar, who reigned about 560 to 556 BC), but that too is uncertain. Riblah, in the land of Hamath on the Orontes River in Syria, served as Nebuchadnezzar's field headquarters.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, a rebel vassal who had broken an oath of loyalty could expect exemplary punishment. Killing a king's sons in front of him ended his dynasty, and blinding him made it the last thing he would ever see; Assyrian and Babylonian records and reliefs show that mutilation of rebels was a known practice. Officials sitting in the city gate (verse 3) was a claim of authority, since the gate was where a city's rulers sat to govern and judge.

The king's garden and the gate between the two walls lay at the southeastern end of the city, near the Kidron and Hinnom valleys, and the road to the Arabah led east down to the Jordan Valley. Zedekiah was probably trying to escape across the Jordan. The policy described in verse 10 was typical of Babylonian practice: remove the leading families, craftsmen, and soldiers, and leave the poor to keep the land farmed and tribute flowing. For the landless poor, receiving vineyards and fields was a reversal of their fortunes.
literary: The chapter is built in three panels. The first (verses 1 to 10) is terse, flat reporting, the style of a royal chronicle, and it closely parallels 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52. The Greek translation of Jeremiah (the Septuagint, made by Jewish scholars in the last centuries BC), which is noticeably shorter than the Hebrew in many places, lacks most of verses 4 to 13, and scholars debate whether the Hebrew added them from Kings or the Greek omitted them. The second panel (verses 11 to 14) turns to Jeremiah's release. The third (verses 15 to 18) steps back in time to a word spoken while Jeremiah was still confined, a flashback placed here so that the chapter ends not with fire but with a promise. The repeated phrase “before his eyes” in verse 6 and “before your eyes” in verse 16 links the two fates: Zedekiah sees judgment fall on his house, and Ebed-melech sees the city fall and lives.

outline.t: The siege and the breach of the wall
The city burned, the people exiled, the poor left

doctrines.note: God's word of judgment, spoken for decades and refused at every turn, comes true in detail. The chapter shows that God's patience is real and that it has an end.
Ebed-melech is spared “Because you have trusted in Me” (verse 18). In a chapter of collapse, the one thing that marks a person for rescue is trust in God.

The loss of king, city, and land is the covenant curse Moses warned of (Deuteronomy 28:36, 64). Yet God had also promised through Jeremiah that he would not make a full end (5:18) and that he would bring his people back.

words.note: Baqa, to split or break open. It describes the wall being breached in verse 2. The same verb is used of God splitting the sea at the exodus (Exodus 14:16); the God who once broke open the waters to free his people now allows the wall to be broken open in judgment.

Batach, to trust, to rely on something for security. Jeremiah repeatedly condemns false trust in the temple (7:4), in Egypt, and in walls. Here, for once, someone trusts in the right place, and God says so.
Natsal, to rescue or snatch away. God promises to rescue Ebed-melech (verse 17), echoing what he had promised Jeremiah at his call: “I am with you to deliver you” (1:8).

Galah, which basically means to uncover and, in this form, to carry into exile (verse 9). Its related noun golah became the name for the exile and for the community of exiles, and the exile becomes the defining event of the rest of the Old Testament.

christ: This chapter is the end of the kingdom of David in Jerusalem. No descendant of David would rule there again as king. That is why the Old Testament promises of a righteous Branch from David's line (23:5-6, 33:14-17) are so striking: they were spoken to a people who would watch the last Davidic king led away blind. The Gospels open by presenting Jesus as the son of David who inherits those promises (Matthew 1:1), and Matthew's genealogy marks the deportation to Babylon as one of the turning points of Israel's history (Matthew 1:11-12, 17). Ebed-melech's rescue also foreshadows something in the gospel: an outsider, not from Israel, saved because he trusted God, a pattern the New Testament sees widened to the nations.

hard.q: In 34:4-5 Jeremiah told Zedekiah he would not die by the sword but would die in peace and be mourned. How does that fit with the brutal treatment in this chapter?
hard.a: The tension is real. Zedekiah was not killed by the sword; he was blinded and held in Babylon until his death (52:11). Some interpreters read the promise of dying in peace as meaning a natural death rather than execution, with a proper burial and mourning, which the prophecy does describe. Others think the promise in chapter 34 was conditional, part of the offer that would have been fulfilled if Zedekiah had surrendered, and that his refusal changed the outcome. A third view notes that Ezekiel 12:13 said Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon but would not see it, which fits his blinding exactly, and that the prophets spoke of his end in terms that were true but not complete. The honest answer is that the text offers no explanation, and readers weigh these possibilities differently.

questions: The fall of Jerusalem came after decades of warnings. Why do people and institutions so often ignore slowly approaching disaster until it is too late?
The poor who had nothing were given fields when the powerful were taken away. Where else in Scripture does God reverse the fortunes of the mighty and the lowly?
Ebed-melech was saved because he trusted God. What did that trust look like in practice, and what might it look like for you?
